How is property tax figured on a Tennessee house?

The county takes the appraised value of the house, converts it to an assessed value with a percentage set in state law, then applies the local rate. For a home that percentage is a quarter of the appraisal. The Comptroller breaks the bill into four parts: appraised value, assessment ratio, assessed value and tax rate.

Take a house appraised at $240,000. Its assessed value comes to $60,000. If local governments charge $2.80 on each hundred dollars of assessed value, the bill is $60,000 divided by 100 and multiplied by 2.80, which equals $1,680. The county commission picks the county rate, and a city governing body adds its own if the home is inside city limits.

A high bill alone gives you nothing to appeal. The Comptroller's guide to assessment and taxation names three grounds: your value is too high, another owner's value is too low, or the property is classified wrongly. A rate increase is outside the assessor's reach, while a jump in the appraisal opens the door to an appeal.

Who sets the value and who collects the tax?

Two separate offices handle a Tennessee property tax bill. The county assessor of property appraises and classifies the parcel. The county trustee, or a city collecting official inside a city, collects the money. State law keeps those jobs apart on purpose, so the person who values your house never sets your rate.

  • The assessor appraises real estate, tracks ownership and boundary changes, and must verify certain facts on real estate sales with the buyer or seller.
  • The county commission and city governing bodies set the tax rates.
  • The State Board of Equalization writes the procedures assessors follow and hears appeals that go past the county level.
  • The Comptroller's Division of Property Assessments monitors assessors and supports them during reappraisal.

Every county revalues all real property on a four, five or six year cycle. Between those revaluations the appraisal generally stays put unless something changes on the parcel, such as a new building, an addition or a demolition. The assessor sends an assessment change notice whenever the value or the classification changes.

What assessment percentages apply to each kind of property?

Residential and farm real property are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, which is the lowest rate on the state's list. Commercial and industrial property is assessed at 40 percent, business personal property at 30 percent and public utility property at 55 percent. A rental house owned by an individual is still residential property, so a landlord selling a Tennessee rental starts from the same 25 percent.

Tennessee assessment percentages by property class. Source: Tennessee Comptroller, Assessment vs Taxation.
Property classShare of appraised value assessed
Residential25%
Farm25%
Commercial and industrial40%
Business personal property30%
Public utility55%

The Comptroller's own example is a residence appraised at $100,000, which carries an assessed value of $25,000. Because counties reappraise on different cycles, the state also builds an equalization factor from an appraisal ratio study so that property valued in different years is compared fairly.

When does a Tennessee property tax bill come due, and when is it late?

Bills for the current year are payable from the first Monday in October. Payment through the end of February avoids interest, and March 1 starts delinquency. The Comptroller's assessment schedule gives each step and the statute behind it.

  • January 1: assessment date, when records must show the property as it stood that day.
  • May 20: change notices should be mailed, and exemption applications are due.
  • June 1: county board of equalization convenes. Shelby County starts on May 1.
  • July: the county sets its rate, and its budget is adopted by July 1.
  • August 1: general cutoff for State Board appeals.
  • February 28: final interest-free day for the prior year's bill.

The bill covers the whole tax year, so a house that sells in spring or summer still has a full year's tax to account for. Ask the county trustee for the current balance before you sign a purchase contract, and have the closing agent explain how buyer and seller will divide the year.

How do I contest a Tennessee property assessment?

Go to the county board of equalization first. A disputed assessment generally becomes final if it never went there, and the county assessor's office explains how to get on the board's calendar. Some assessors will review a value informally, yet the State Board says that review does not count as an appeal and does not protect your later rights.

  • County board: five or more members who hear taxpayer complaints and can change a disputed assessment.
  • State Board filing window: by August 1 of the tax year or 45 days after the county board's notice went out, whichever falls later. You file online.
  • Hearing: notice arrives at least 60 days before the date, and an Administrative Judge rules within 90 days afterward.
  • Finality: the judge's order typically becomes final 30 days after signing when no one seeks more review.
  • Chancery court: a petition is due 60 days after the board's order is final.

The burden rests on you to show the correct value by a preponderance of the evidence. For houses, the board treats sales of comparable properties as the strongest proof, with differences in acreage, square footage, age, condition and location explained and adjusted. Saying the house is overvalued, with nothing to back a number, rarely succeeds. An appraisal may be offered, and the appraiser may be asked to testify.

Five situations let an owner go straight to the State Board: no proper notice of an increase, a change notice mailed fewer than ten days before the county board adjourned, reasonable cause outside your control, an appeal of a correction the assessor made or refused, and written assessor consent for commercial or industrial property. No appeal is accepted after March 1 of the year after the appeal period began to run.

Must I pay taxes while an appeal is open?

Pay at least the undisputed portion before delinquency begins. The State Board's page shows the arithmetic, which starts from the value you claim in good faith, and the county trustee can give you the number for your parcel. Delinquent taxes for earlier years must also be paid in full, or the appeal can stall or be dismissed.

If a certificate of assessment later leaves you short, you owe the difference plus interest at the Federal Reserve composite prime rate minus two points. Penalty and interest held back during the appeal start to accrue 30 days after a decision becomes final. Refunds go out within 60 days of the appeal closing, and extra payments come due within 30 days of closing.

Which programs reduce the bill for Tennessee homeowners?

Three programs matter to a homeowner: the state's tax relief reimbursement, a local option freeze for owners 65 and older, and greenbelt classification for qualifying farm, forest and open space land. Relief repays taxes you already paid, so the bill still arrives. For 2026 the Comptroller lists a $38,470 income cap for elderly and disabled applicants, with applications due 35 days after the local delinquency date, which falls in April.

Greenbelt applications are due March 15, and the assessor can explain the rollback assessment that may follow a change in land use. Our Tennessee homestead exemption guide goes through relief and freeze rules in detail. The statute limits relief to one residence per tax year, so an owner who moves should ask the trustee how the new address is handled.

What should a seller check about tax before listing a Tennessee house?

Call the county trustee, and the city collecting official when the house sits inside a city, and ask for a payoff figure on the parcel. The Tennessee Property Assessment Database shows the appraisal and classification, so a wrong classification can be caught early. If an appeal is pending, the trustee can say what has been paid and what remains.

An owner planning to appeal should know the State Board expects delinquent taxes from earlier years to be paid in full. A buyer who purchases as-is will weigh any open balance in the price, and you are welcome to ask us for an offer while a bill is open.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Tennessee property tax rate?

No single statewide rate exists. Each county commission and city governing body sets its own, expressed in dollars per hundred of assessed value, and a residence is assessed at one quarter of its appraisal. The Comptroller publishes local rates, and your county trustee can tell you the combined figure for an address.

Can I still appeal this year's assessment?

The usual 2026 dates have passed. Change notices were due out by May 20, the county board met from June 1, and the State Board's general filing date was August 1, though a later county board notice can extend it to 45 days after the notice. Ask your assessor now for next year's county board date and watch for the spring change notice.

Can I appeal because my bill went up?

Only when the increase comes from the appraisal or classification. The Comptroller says a tax amount is not a valid basis for appeal, and neither the assessor nor the state board can change a rate set by the county commission.

Do I need a lawyer for an assessment appeal?

No. The State Board says you may appear alone or bring a representative such as an attorney or authorized agent. An assessor's representative usually attends, and the Administrative Judge decides only on the evidence presented.

What happens if I miss the payment date?

Interest starts once February ends, and March 1 begins delinquency. Penalty and interest continue to run unless an appeal is pending and you paid the undisputed portion. Ask the county trustee for the exact balance and options on your parcel.

Does Tennessee have a homestead exemption on property tax?

Tennessee does not give owners a homestead exemption that removes part of a home's value from the tax roll. What it offers instead is a state reimbursement program called property tax relief, plus a local option tax freeze. The Comptroller describes relief as a reimbursement, and a court of appeals case noted in the statute annotations says the relief statute is not an exemption statute at all: the property stays taxable and the city and county receive the full tax.

Tennessee also has a separate homestead rule in Title 26 that protects equity from creditors. People often confuse the two, and a seller dealing with both a tax bill and a debt may need to look at each one. This page covers the tax programs first and the creditor protection after that.

Who qualifies for Tennessee property tax relief in 2026?

Low-income homeowners who are 65 or older, homeowners who are totally and permanently disabled, and certain disabled veterans or their surviving spouses can qualify. The program began in 1973 and is paid from state appropriations. You apply through the county trustee, or the city collecting official if the property is inside a city.

  • Elderly: you must be 65 on or before December 31 of the application year, own the home, and use it as your primary residence.
  • Disabled: you must be disabled on or before December 31 of the application year, with the same ownership and residence tests.
  • Disabled veteran: you must complete a 2026 Form F-16, which releases disability and income information from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.
  • Surviving spouse of a disabled veteran: you must complete Form F-16S, provide a death certificate and personal ID, and not have remarried.
2026 Tennessee property tax relief limits. Source: Tennessee Comptroller 2026 brochure.
GroupIncome capMarket value on which relief is figured
Elderly homeowner$38,470 (2025 income)$33,600
Disabled homeowner$38,470 (2025 income)$33,600
Disabled veteran or qualifying surviving spouseNo income limit$175,000

The income that counts is the combined income of all owners, the applicant's spouse, and any resident owner of a remainder interest. A sole owner within $100 of the cap, or a household with a co-owner within $200 of the cap, must document income from every source. Social security, railroad retirement and veterans benefits that must be paid to a nursing home are not counted for an owner who moves into one.

When and where do I apply for relief?

You apply when your 2026 tax bill arrives, and the deadline is 35 days after the local delinquency date. Because delinquency begins March 1, that deadline falls in April. The Comptroller's schedule shows the same April date, and local officials forward applications to the state, which normally expects them by May 5.

A county trustee can give a credit on the bill if the application looks eligible, provided you pay the balance. Statute does not require the whole bill to be paid by the delinquency date as a condition of eligibility, though the brochure tells applicants that taxes must also be paid by the deadline, so confirm with the trustee how your county handles it. The director of the Division of Property Assessments may waive a missed deadline for good and reasonable cause, but never past December 31 of the year after the tax year.

You can check an application's status on the Comptroller's website, or call the Property Tax Relief office at 615.747.8871. The office sits in the Cordell Hull Building in Nashville.

How does the Tennessee property tax freeze work?

A freeze locks the tax on a principal residence at the amount owed in the first year the owner qualifies. Afterward the amount generally stays the same even if the rate rises or the county reappraises. The General Assembly passed the Property Tax Freeze Act in 2007, and each county or city chooses whether to adopt it.

  • You must own your principal residence in a participating county or city and be 65 by the end of the year you file.
  • Your income from all sources must stay under the limit for your county, and you reapply every year with proof of income, age and ownership.
  • The freeze covers the home and no more than 5 acres. Taxes on commercial, farm or forest portions are not frozen.
  • If the actual calculated tax falls below the frozen amount, you pay the lower amount and the frozen figure resets downward.
  • The benefit adds to the relief program, but it requires its own application.

The Comptroller counted 28 counties and 37 cities on the 2026 list. Local option limits are tied to a $60,000 base set for 2024 and moved by the Social Security cost of living adjustment, reaching $63,470 for 2026.

Sample 2026 income limits from the Comptroller's freeze list: Davidson, Knox and Shelby counties and the city of Chattanooga $63,470; Williamson County $69,150; Madison County $51,620.

What happens to relief or a freeze when I sell?

The freeze does not travel with you. The Comptroller says the base amount changes when an owner sells and buys another residence, and benefits must be established separately for each property. Improvements to the home raise the frozen base in proportion to the added value.

For the freeze, you do not need to have owned the home on January 1, but you must have owned it for part of the year and still own it on the application deadline. If a qualified applicant dies mid-year, taxes stay frozen for the whole year. Under the relief statute, a surviving spouse can present a voucher chosen by a deceased applicant and receive the final payment, unless the taxes were paid before the death.

Relief is limited to one residence and one recipient per property for each tax year. A person who gave false income information must repay the state, with penalty and interest. Someone paid in error generally must repay if the state makes demand within two years of the due date for that tax year. Before listing, ask the trustee whether you have a pending voucher or credit on the parcel so that closing figures match.

What does the $35,000 state homestead protect?

Tennessee Code section 26-2-301 lets an individual protect up to $35,000 of homestead equity from creditors, and joint owners claiming together can protect $52,500. A 2021 amendment raised those amounts from $5,000 and $7,500, effective January 1, 2022. The General Assembly's fiscal memorandum on SB 566 and HB 676 also raised the amount of sale surplus exempt for a surviving spouse or minor children from $5,000 to $35,000.

The same amendment removed the higher tiers that once existed for owners 62 or older and for owners with minor children. The memorandum adds that, under section 26-2-306, homestead exemptions do not apply to property tax liens. A tax bill is therefore outside what this protection reaches.

This creditor protection comes into play when a lender or other creditor goes after the house. It has no application form like the tax programs do. An attorney can tell you how it interacts with a mortgage, a judgment or a bankruptcy filing.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Tennessee homestead exemption that lowers my property tax?

No. Tennessee's closest program is property tax relief, which reimburses taxes after you pay them, and the local tax freeze, which caps the amount owed. Neither removes value from the assessment. The $35,000 state homestead only protects equity from creditors and does not apply to property tax liens.

How much income can I have and still get 2026 relief?

The 2026 Comptroller brochure sets the limit at $38,470 for elderly and disabled homeowners, based on 2025 income for the applicant, spouse, co-owner and resident remainder owner. Relief is figured on up to $33,600 of market value. Disabled veterans and qualifying surviving spouses have no income limit.

What is the deadline to apply?

Apply within 35 days after the local property tax delinquency date, and pay your taxes by that deadline as the brochure instructs. Since delinquency starts March 1, the cutoff lands in April. The state director can waive a missed deadline for good cause until December 31 of the following year.

Can I use the freeze in any county?

Only in counties and cities that adopted it. The Comptroller's list shows 28 counties and 37 cities, and each has its own income limit for 2026. Ask your county trustee or city collecting official whether your address is covered.

Does the homestead protect me from unpaid property taxes?

No. The fiscal memorandum for the 2021 amendment points to section 26-2-306, which makes homestead exemptions inapplicable to property tax liens. Contact the county trustee about the balance on your parcel.

title: Tennessee Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Is there still a Tennessee tax on what heirs receive?

No. Tennessee's inheritance tax is gone for anyone who died in 2016 or after. The Department of Revenue's page says the levy is no longer imposed after December 31, 2015, and it asks families not to file for those later deaths.

Back when it applied, the tax reached the portion of the net estate above an exemption tied to the year of death. Net estate meant the market value of every asset after subtracting items such as property passing to a surviving spouse, debts and administration costs, and the executor, administrator or trustee paid the bill from estate funds. A family listing an inherited house in Tennessee today skips that return entirely. The federal estate tax is the only one left, and it reaches very large estates.

At what size does the federal estate tax reach a Tennessee estate?

Only at a very high threshold. According to the IRS, the Working Families Tax Cuts law, Public Law 119-21 signed July 4, 2025, lifts the basic exclusion amount to $15,000,000 for 2026. Recent years looked like this.

Year of deathBasic exclusion amount
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Source: IRS, What's new, estate and gift tax. The IRS notes the top bracket rate has stood at 40 percent since 2013. A typical Tennessee family house falls far under these numbers, so most estates never send a Form 706. Total the house with bank balances, retirement accounts and insurance owned at death before deciding no return is needed.

Can a widow or widower carry over the unused federal amount?

Yes. For decedents with a surviving spouse, an estate may elect, starting January 1, 2011, to pass the decedent's unused exclusion to that spouse. The election sits on a timely filed estate tax return, so a Form 706 can pay off even where no tax is owed.

The IRS adds that simplified valuation rules cover estates that would not need to file apart from the election. A surviving spouse in Tennessee who plans to sell the family home and hold a large portfolio should raise this with the estate's lawyer well ahead of the filing deadline.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Tennessee house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Which value do heirs use when they sell an inherited Tennessee house?

They use the home's worth at the owner's death. IRS Publication 551 says inherited property generally takes its market value on that day, or on the alternate valuation date if the executor picked one. Suppose a house was worth $240,000 at death and sells for $245,000. The federal gain is $5,000, whatever the decedent paid decades earlier.

  • An estate that had to file a federal return gives each beneficiary a Schedule A (Form 8971) stating the estate tax value.
  • The IRS issued final regulations on September 16, 2024 for consistent basis reporting between an estate and a person acquiring property from it.
  • An estate under the filing requirement should skip Form 8971, since the IRS warns that sending it can produce needless letters.

For a smaller estate, hire a licensed appraiser to value the house as of the death and keep that report with the estate file.

What if a child gave the house to a parent shortly before the parent died?

The rule changes in this narrow case. Publication 551 carves out appreciated property that you or your spouse handed to the decedent during the final year of life; the death-day value does not govern it. When it comes back to you, your basis equals the decedent's adjusted basis immediately before death.

Appreciated property means an item whose market value on the day of the gift beat the giver's adjusted basis. Tennessee families who retitle a house to a relative and then inherit it back should talk with the estate's attorney first, so the tax effect is clear before anyone signs a deed.

Who owes the recording tax when the estate sells the house?

The buyer owes it, as the grantee. The Department of Revenue's recordation tax page says the county register of deeds gathers the tax, and its rate table sets realty transfer tax at $0.37 per $100 of purchase price. An estate sale at $180,000 therefore carries $666.

Property tax follows separate steps. The Comptroller's overview of assessment and taxation has the county assessor appraising the parcel, the county commission and city governing bodies fixing rates, and the county trustee and city officials collecting. Request the parcel's open balance from the trustee's office and pass it to the closing agent.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Tennessee houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How will the county value the inherited house for property tax?

The assessor applies a 25 percent ratio to residential appraisals, so a $100,000 appraisal becomes a $25,000 assessment. Appraisals reset during reappraisal programs on a 6, 5 or 4 year cycle and generally hold steady between them unless buildings change.

  • An owner can challenge an overstated value, an understated value on someone else's parcel, or the way the parcel is classified.
  • Complaints about the dollar amount of the bill are not accepted as a reason.
  • The sequence runs from a conversation with the assessor to the county equalization board, which opens its sessions June 1, and on to the state board and Chancery Court.

An heir who receives an older house last appraised years ago may see a new number at the next reappraisal.

What papers should heirs gather before listing?

A tidy folder shortens closing and supports the basis you report later. Assemble these before the sign goes up.

  • A certified death certificate and the court order naming the person authorized to sign the deed.
  • The appraisal as of the death, or the Schedule A if a Form 706 was filed.
  • The newest tax bill, plus a payoff number from the trustee.
  • Receipts for additions the decedent paid for, because the IRS counts improvements that add value toward basis.
  • A payoff statement from any lender.

Give the title company copies early so the closer can tell whether the signer needs more authority than the folder shows. Missing court paperwork is a common reason an estate closing slips by days or weeks, so ask the clerk for certified copies in advance.

IRS Topic no. 409 mentions that a taxable gain can call for estimated tax payments, so ask the preparer about due dates once an offer is accepted.

Does an estate sale bring any other small tax item?

Two items can come up. The IRS fee for an estate tax closing letter, Letter 627, rose from $56 to $76 effective October 26, 2026, and it matters only to estates that filed a Form 706. The yearly gift exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2026, which can matter if a parent was moving the house to children before death.

On the court side, ask the clerk where the decedent lived which office handles letters of administration or probate of a will. That office can explain what the court must approve before a sale.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does Tennessee charge inheritance tax in 2026?

It does not. The Department of Revenue says the tax ended after December 31, 2015, and no return is due for deaths in 2016 or later.

What federal estate tax threshold applies this year?

For deaths in 2026 the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person, under Public Law 119-21. A surviving spouse can add the unused portion through an election on a timely filed return.

What starting value do heirs use for an inherited house?

Generally what the house was worth on the day the owner died. Any gain is measured from that figure.

Whose job is it to pay the deed tax on an estate sale?

The buyer pays $0.37 for each $100 of price when the deed is filed with the register.

Can heirs contest the county's value of an inherited house?

Yes, for a value set too high or a wrong classification. Talk to the assessor first, then take it to the county equalization board, which opens June 1.

What does a Tennessee quitclaim deed do?

It hands over whatever the signer owns, with no assurance that the signer owns anything. Tennessee's revenue department describes a true quitclaim as passing only a "mere chance of title," and it contrasts that with a deed that conveys the property itself or gives a warranty.

Families use quitclaims to move a house between relatives, to add or drop a spouse, and to remove a name from a chain of ownership. Since no warranty rides along, anyone who accepts one from a stranger is leaning entirely on the title search. If you intend to sell, expect a title company to look harder at a house whose last transfer was a quitclaim than at one with a warranty deed behind it.

Whatever the deed type, it only gains public standing once the county register of deeds records it. That is the stage where Tennessee's tax, fee and formatting rules bite, and the sections below follow it step by step.

How much recording tax does a Tennessee quitclaim deed carry?

The state realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of value, which works out to $3.70 per $1,000. The grantee owes it, and the register in the receiving county collects it at the counter. The Department of Revenue rate page confirms the figure.

A quitclaim differs in what the rate is multiplied by. Shelby County's register states that only the consideration actually given is used for a quitclaim, citing Tenn. Code Ann. 67-4-409(a)(1)(D). A quitclaim signed for $10 between relatives therefore produces a tiny bill, while a deed worded to reach the property itself is taxed on its worth.

How a deed's wording picks the tax base
What the deed says or doesTax base
Passes only the signer's chance of titleConsideration given
Contains a habendum clause ("to have and to hold") or says "in fee simple (absolute)"Fair market value
Falls in a statutory exemptionNo tax and no oath of value

As a worked example, a $250,000 house taxed at full value would owe $925 (250,000 times 0.0037). The same house conveyed by a true quitclaim for $10 of consideration would owe pennies at that rate, and the register's page fees would still apply.

Which quitclaim wording pushes the tax up to fair market value?

Any phrase that signals an intent to convey the land itself, or that promises title, shifts the base from consideration to value. Revenue's two examples are the habendum clause and "in fee simple (absolute)," and it says the list is open-ended.

Drafting is therefore part of tax planning. A downloaded form with warranty-style phrases can turn a cheap transfer into an expensive one, so ask whoever prepares the deed to strip them out if you want the lower base. Deeds drawn by an attorney or title company should already match the treatment you expect.

  • Read the granting clause for words that promise good title.
  • Look for a habendum clause or fee simple language.
  • Make sure the stated consideration matches what changed hands.
  • Ask the register to explain the tax before you leave the deed there.

How is fair market value measured when the deed is taxed on value?

Revenue accepts the base on the assessor's books or a recent appraisal that the assessor has accepted in a dispute over the base. A lower figure invites an audit, with penalties and interest on anything found owing.

So the appraised value on your county roll is the safest starting number. If you think it runs high, an assessor-approved appraisal is the route to challenge it. Request the parcel's current appraisal from the county assessor before the deed is drawn, so the sworn value and the tax paid agree.

What paperwork does a register want with a quitclaim deed?

Shelby County's register publishes a checklist with statute cites for each line, and the list marks every line below as applying to quitclaim deeds. Other counties draw on the same Tennessee statutes, though each register runs its own counter.

  • The names of both the grantor and the grantee.
  • A sworn statement of value whenever the deed is taxable.
  • A derivation clause naming how the grantor took title, and the street address unless the land is vacant.
  • The owner's name and address, plus whoever pays the property tax bill.
  • The ward, block and parcel number and a full legal description.
  • The name and address of whoever prepared the deed (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-24-115).
  • Notarized signatures and an original, unless the filing goes in electronically.

Davidson County's fee page repeats the preparer rule in one sentence: every document except releases and charters must show who drafted it. Phone the register where the house is located and ask how that office takes submissions before you drive over with a deed.

What will filing a quitclaim deed set you back in Nashville and Memphis?

Fees flow from Tenn. Code Ann. 8-21-1001. Davidson County puts warranty and quitclaim deeds under "all other documents" at $5 a page, a $10 floor and a $2 data processing charge. Shelby County bills $10 for the first two pages and $5 for each later page, with its own data processing line.

  • Davidson County adds a $1 probate fee that applies only when state tax is paid.
  • Shelby County adds a $1 register fee under the same condition.
  • The $0.37 per $100 tax in both counties is billed on top of the page fees.

Other counties publish their own schedules, so ask the register of the county that holds your parcel for the current numbers.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Tennessee houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which transfers owe no recording tax?

Several do, and Shelby County's guide lists them under 67-4-409(a)(1). Where a deed falls in an exempt class, no oath of value is demanded either.

  • One spouse conveying to the other to create or end a tenancy by the entirety.
  • Deeds that settle property between divorcing spouses.
  • Moves into a revocable living trust by its creator or the creator's spouse, and moves back out.
  • An executor's deed that carries out a devise in a will.

An exemption removes the tax and the oath. It leaves the fee schedule and the formatting rules in place.

Did Tennessee change what registers can record in 2026?

It did. Public Chapter 865 amends Tenn. Code Ann. 66-24-101(a), and the University of Tennessee's County Technical Assistance Service lists it in its 2026 index of acts with an April 27, 2026 effective date.

A bond for conveying real or personal property now needs every bound party's authenticated signature and the bond's expiration date to be recordable. Sale agreements, contracts, memoranda and abstracts for real property need the authenticated signatures of the owner (or the owner's attorney-in-fact or court-appointed representative) and the proposed purchaser, plus an expiration date. A quitclaim deed is a separate instrument, yet a seller who records a contract or memorandum should plan around the stricter standard.

Frequently asked questions

Who has to pay Tennessee's tax on a quitclaim deed?

The grantee. Revenue's help article says the person receiving the interest pays, and that the register of the county where the deed is recorded collects it.

Does a quitclaim deed need a sworn statement of value?

Yes when the deed is taxable. Shelby County's checklist lists an affidavit of value under 67-4-409(a)(6)(A) and says exempt transactions need no oath.

Can spouses use a quitclaim without paying tax?

A conveyance from one spouse to the other that creates or ends a tenancy by the entirety is exempt, and so are deeds between divorcing spouses. The exemptions are narrow, so check your facts with the register or an attorney.

What does the clerk charge in Nashville to file a quitclaim deed?

Davidson County charges $5 a page with a $10 minimum and a $2 data processing fee. A $1 probate fee and the $0.37 per $100 transfer tax come on top when state tax is due.

Will a register take a photocopy of my quitclaim deed?

Generally no. Shelby County asks for an original unless the filing is made electronically, so ask your own register whether it offers e-filing.

content:
Tennessee Transfer on Death Deed: How It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Tennessee
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Tennessee Transfer on Death Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Tennessee Transfer on Death Deed sale
  • Turn the Tennessee Transfer on Death Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Tennessee House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Tennessee?
We buy Tennessee houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Is a TOD deed available to Tennessee homeowners?

Lawmakers have been asked to create one. Senate Bill 984 in the 114th General Assembly proposed a "Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act," and House Bill 1793 with Senate Bill 2029 brought a reworked version to the 2026 session. Before signing any such form, ask the register in your county or a Tennessee attorney whether a TOD deed can be recorded today.

The bill text is still worth reading, because it shows the design the Legislature has been shown: a deed that names a beneficiary, works only if it is on record before the owner dies, and leaves the owner free to sell or borrow in the meantime. After that, this page turns to the recording rules that already apply to any deed filed in Tennessee.

What would the proposed deed have to say?

Senate Bill 984 lists three musts, and the 2026 bills carry them forward. The instrument has to meet the usual formalities for a recordable deed, say that the beneficiary receives the property when the owner dies, and be filed with the register where the land lies before that death.

  • Mental capacity: measured by the standard for making a will.
  • Notice to the beneficiary, delivery, acceptance and payment: none is needed.
  • Title promises: the deed passes the property without any warranty, even if its text claims one.
  • Sample form: the bill prints a "Revocable Transfer on Death Deed" with spaces for owner names, mailing addresses, marital status, legal description, a primary and an alternate beneficiary, signatures and a notary's acknowledgment.

Senate Bill 984 also edits Tenn. Code Ann. 66-24-101(a)(12) so TOD deeds appear among the instruments a register may accept.

How is the deed undone, and what does it change while the owner lives?

Undoing it takes a recorded writing. Under Senate Bill 984, a revocation counts only if the owner acknowledged it after signing the earlier deed and it was recorded before death in the same county. Three kinds of paper qualify: a newer TOD deed that cancels the first expressly or by conflict, a stand-alone revocation, or an ordinary deed that says it revokes the TOD deed. Scribbling on the recorded deed does nothing, and the sample form adds that a will cannot revoke it. If several joint owners signed, every living joint owner must join the revocation.

While the owner is alive, the bill keeps the deed quiet. It leaves the owner's power to sell or mortgage untouched, leaves a buyer's rights intact even if the buyer knows of the deed, leaves creditors where they were, and gives the beneficiary no legal or equitable share. Eligibility for public assistance is unaffected unless federal law says otherwise.

The plain-language notes on the form give practical advice. Record in every county that holds part of the land. Destroy an unrecorded deed if you change your mind. Do not complete the form under pressure from anyone. Tell the beneficiaries, since secrecy can make fraud easier.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Tennessee house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens to the mortgage and the creditors when the owner dies?

The beneficiary inherits the house with its baggage: mortgages, liens, contracts and any TennCare claim for medical assistance. The gift also depends on survival. A beneficiary who dies first loses the share, and when several people were named, a lapsed share goes to the others in proportion.

Creditors keep a path to the house. If the probate estate falls short of paying allowed claims or the spouse's and children's statutory allowances, the estate or a creditor can pursue property that passed under the deed. Senate Bill 984 allows eighteen months from death to start that case. The summary of Senate Bill 2029 narrows the period to twelve months and says that when the beneficiary has already sold the house, the creditor may go after the beneficiary up to the value conveyed.

For a family planning to sell an inherited house, that means the sale must still pay off the loan and any recorded liens. The deed spares the family a probate filing for the transfer itself, but debts still ride with the property.

How do the 2025 and 2026 bills differ?

TOD deed bills in the 114th General Assembly
PointSB 984 (2025)HB 1793 / SB 2029 (2026)
Applies to owners dying on or afterJuly 1, 2025July 1, 2026
Deed labeled nontestamentaryYesYes
Window for creditors to act against the property18 months after death12 months after death
Creditor action against a beneficiary who already soldNot addressed in the bill textBeneficiary liable up to the value conveyed
Beneficiary designation on vehicle titlesIncludedIncluded

Source: bill summaries and text on the Tennessee General Assembly site, where the current status of each measure is posted.

What would filing such a deed cost in Davidson County?

A TOD deed, if it becomes recordable, would pass through the same fee table as any other deed under Tenn. Code Ann. 8-21-1001. Nashville's register charges $5 per page for deeds, with a $10 floor and a $2 data processing charge, and it wants the drafter's name and address on almost everything it records.

The state transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 according to the revenue department. The Senate bill says the deed is valid without consideration, so whether any transfer tax follows when the beneficiary takes title is a question for the register or an attorney once the law is settled.

Shelby County prices the same document differently on its face: $10 for the first two pages and $5 for each page after that, plus a data processing fee. Check the page count before you print, and ask whether the office accepts the deed by e-filing or only in person.

  • A $1 probate fee in Davidson County, collected only when state tax is paid.
  • The drafter's name and address on the face of the document.
  • Releases and charters are the only documents excused from that last rule.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Tennessee houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What can an owner do today to avoid probate?

Sit down with a Tennessee attorney and bring the vesting deed, the legal description and a list of everyone you want to provide for. Some family and trust transfers are already exempt from the transfer tax; Shelby County's register lists moves into a revocable living trust by its creator, and trustee deeds that carry out a testamentary devise, under 67-4-409(a)(1).

If the house has already been inherited and you want to sell it, the practical questions are who holds title and whether a court has named anyone to act for the estate. Ask the register where the house sits how documents must be formatted, and ask an attorney how title passes in your family's situation.

Frequently asked questions

Is a TOD deed legal in Tennessee?

Lawmakers have taken up bills to authorize one, including Senate Bill 984 in 2025 and House Bill 1793 with Senate Bill 2029 in 2026. Check with the register or a Tennessee attorney before relying on any form.

Must the deed be on record before death?

Yes, under the bills. It has to be filed with the register in the county where the property lies while the owner is alive, or it has no effect.

Can I still sell after I sign?

The bill text says the deed leaves the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property alone, and the beneficiary holds no legal or equitable interest until the owner dies.

Does the beneficiary get the house debt free?

No. The house passes subject to mortgages, liens and TennCare claims, and creditors may reach it when the estate falls short.

How does an owner cancel a recorded TOD deed?

With a recorded, acknowledged writing: a later TOD deed, a revocation form, or a deed that expressly revokes it. Marking up the old deed or naming the change in a will does not work under the bill.

Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Tennessee
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Tennessee Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Tennessee House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Tennessee?
We buy Tennessee houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Will Tennessee take a share of my profit when I sell a house?

No. Tennessee collects nothing from a seller's profit at the state level. The Department of Revenue says its former Hall income tax reached only interest from bonds and notes and dividends from stock, and that levy ended for tax periods starting January 1, 2021 and later. The Department's help center separately states that wages, employer retirement income and most other forms of income carry no Tennessee individual income tax.

The tax question for a Tennessee seller is therefore a federal one. If a company or partnership holds title instead of a person, call the Department before you pick a closing date, since entity taxes are a different subject from the personal tax described here.

How much profit can a Tennessee homeowner shield from federal tax?

A single owner can shield the first $250,000 of profit on a main home, and spouses filing together can shield $500,000. IRS Topic no. 701 sets two requirements, ownership and use. Each must be satisfied for at least 24 months within the five years that end on the closing date, and the months need not overlap.

  • Spouses filing jointly need only one of them to pass the ownership test, but each must pass the use test personally.
  • An exclusion claimed on a different house in the preceding two years generally blocks a second one.
  • Members of the uniformed services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community on qualified extended duty may elect to pause the five year clock for as long as ten years.

IRS Publication 523 supplies worksheets and the list of exceptions. Read it before assuming a sale in Knoxville, Memphis or a small Tennessee town creates no tax.

Do I still file anything if the whole profit is sheltered?

Sometimes. A Form 1099-S from the title company obliges you to report the sale even when none of the profit is taxable, according to the IRS. Reporting is also required if any slice of the profit sits above your limit.

The entry goes on Form 8949, which feeds Schedule D of Form 1040. Gather your closing statement from the original purchase, the settlement sheet from this sale and receipts for lasting improvements. Topic no. 703 defines basis as generally the cost of the asset, raised by improvements that add value and lowered by items such as depreciation and casualty reimbursements. A new roof or finished basement can trim the profit you report.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Tennessee house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What federal rates hit profit beyond the shelter?

Profit on a house owned longer than a year is long-term. The IRS says most of it is taxed at no more than 15 percent for most individuals. The figures below come from IRS Topic no. 409 and describe taxable years beginning in 2025, so confirm the numbers for the year your Tennessee closing occurs.

Filing status0% rate through15% rate through
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700
Married filing separately$48,350$300,000

Income above the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent. A house sold within a year of purchase produces a short-term result, which is taxed like ordinary pay.

How does the calendar affect a Tennessee seller's result?

Topic no. 409 explains how the holding period is counted. You count from the day after you acquired the asset through the day you disposed of it, and more than one year makes the result long-term. A seller who closes on a Tennessee house two days short of the anniversary can move from the lower long-term brackets into ordinary income rates.

The same page raises two further points for owners who exceed the shelter. People with significant investment income may owe the net investment income tax, described in Topic no. 559, and a taxable gain can require estimated tax payments during the year of sale. It also states that a loss on a personal home is not deductible, so a sale below your cost brings no write off.

Do heirs who sell a Tennessee house owe tax on the whole price?

No, because heirs usually start from the home's worth at the owner's death rather than from the owner's old purchase price. Publication 551 says inherited property generally takes its market value on the day of death, or the value six months later when the executor selected the alternate valuation date. A sale near that figure leaves little profit to tax.

  • When the estate filed a federal return, each beneficiary generally gets a Schedule A (Form 8971) stating the value to use.
  • Without a Schedule A, Publication 551 allows the appraised value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.
  • Property you gave to someone who died within the next year, then received back, keeps the giver's basis.

Order an appraisal that names the date of death. It becomes your record on Schedule D.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Tennessee houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What does Tennessee charge on the deed when the house changes hands?

The state levies a realty transfer tax through recordation. Its published rate is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, which works out to $1,110 on a $300,000 sale. A county register collects the money and passes it along. The Department places the obligation on the grantee, the person taking title.

Lenders add a mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of debt after the first $2,000, and the borrower owes it. Phone your county's recording office to learn how it wants the purchase price shown on the deed.

How do payment plans and former rentals change the picture?

Seller financing spreads the profit across years. IRS Topic no. 705 treats any sale with a payment arriving after the year of closing as an installment sale, reported on Form 6252 unless you elect out. You count as income only the portion of each payment that exceeds your basis, while interest is ordinary income.

A house that served as a rental carries depreciation. Publication 551 fixes the depreciable basis at the smaller of the market value when rental use began or your adjusted basis then. Topic no. 409 adds that unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property can be taxed at a top rate of 25 percent. A Tennessee landlord with a former home should ask a preparer for a projection before accepting an offer.

Which official pages hold the current figures?

Tax amounts shift each year, so confirm them at the source before you sign a contract.

  • IRS Topic no. 701 and Publication 523 for the main home exclusion.
  • IRS Topic no. 409 for rates and reporting forms.
  • IRS Publication 551 for inherited and gifted property.
  • Tennessee Department of Revenue pages for recordation tax and the Hall tax.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does Tennessee have a state tax on profit from selling a home?

Tennessee has no personal income tax on wages or most other income, and its Hall tax on interest and dividends stopped for periods beginning January 1, 2021. Federal rules still decide whether any profit is taxable.

How large is the profit shelter for a main home?

It is $250,000 for one owner and $500,000 on a joint return. You need 24 months of ownership plus 24 months of living there inside the five years before closing.

Will heirs be taxed on everything they get from a house sale?

Only on profit above the stepped-up starting value, generally the market value at death. Keep a dated appraisal on file with the estate papers.

What does Tennessee charge on a deed at closing?

The realty transfer tax runs $0.37 for every $100 of price, and the Department of Revenue says the person receiving the deed pays it.

Do I have to file a return for a sale with no taxable profit?

Only when you were sent a Form 1099-S or part of the profit exceeds your limit. In that case the sale goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D.
